replies.text:
The material has four main kinds of documents, plus a few supporting ones.

The first kind is the plan map and the goal statement. `README.md` is the entry point for the whole rebuild plan: it lays out which file answers which question, names the eleven blocks taken from the baseline `plugins/` tree, gives the routing rules for where an item belongs, defines the item format and ID prefixes, lists the attribution forms, and records what sources were audited and what the audit could not cover. `goal.md` is the brief for the rebuild itself. It states the product (three plugins on vanilla Claude Code 2.1.327), the rules the work must follow, and what "done" means, so it is the document that says what to do and when to stop.

The second kind is the requirements documents, which the README places under `prd/`. They follow the ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 outline. `prd/README.md` holds purpose, scope in and out, interfaces, limits, and deferred work, while each `prd/<block>.md` holds one requirement per checkbox item with its acceptance check, verification method, basis, status, and source. These are the items that get ticked off during the rebuild. They are not included in the material shown here, only described.

The third kind is the architecture decision records in `adr/`, which are the bulk of what was provided. Each file follows the MADR layout with a status, a date, the problem, the options considered, the decision, the consequences, and a source line. They record why a choice was made, including user decisions with dates, and some are marked superseded by a later record, such as ADR-0006 and ADR-0010 giving way to ADR-0031 on Monitor. Many rest on a user answer, a transcript line, or a measured probe, and the source line says which.

The fourth kind is the arc42 architecture documentation and the risk register, which the README describes but the material does not include. The arc42 sections cover constraints, Claude Code seams, solution strategy, building blocks, runtime algorithms, deployment, cross-block concepts, quality scenarios, and a glossary. The `risk-register/<block>.md` files record known agent or product faults, each with a cure, scored by likelihood and impact under the ISO 31000 fields.

A supporting document is `reference/you-should-know-prompt.md`, a verbatim copy of a built-in plugin's prompt, kept so that `claudetto-you-should-know` can recreate it exactly.

END-OF-REPLY

The risk register itself is not in the material, so these come from the README's audit notes and the ADRs, and I have not scored them.

The most pervasive risk is lost or weak evidence. The README says the session logs dated 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-16 are no longer on disk, so many citations can only be backed by git history. Twelve logs cited by 8-character id are gone, 145 items have source lines that were not found, and 13 items were removed because no source could be located. The audit also admits its limits: Haiku search workers thrashed, some batches matched by keyword only, one worker read Reddit threads in reduced text, and several dedupe workers checked version claims by grepping release notes instead of probing. Since goal.md requires every fact to be verified by a probe on 2.1.327, a claim resting on a skipped check could be wrong without anyone noticing.

A second risk is silently defeating Claude Code's own safeguards. ADR-0025 records that rewriting a tool input in 2.1.319 voids auto mode's server review, so every call in that response comes back with no verdict. That is why the design denies with the exact form instead of rewriting. ADR-0017 is similar: Jev may deny or ask but never allow, because jevwire is not hardened against injection, so an injected text could otherwise open a gate.

A third risk is hooks that hide their own failures. ADR-0035 notes that 64 of 92 catches bound no error and concealed defects, and that a bare `catch { return [] }` turned a bad grader answer into a clean reply. Guards without a catch fail open on a throw or on an overrun past 10 seconds, so a broken gate can look the same as a passing one. The ADR is itself superseded, so the current policy needs checking against ADR-0168.

A fourth risk is tools that destroy user work. ADR-0036 reproduced `oxlint --fix-suggestions` deleting 81 `console.log` calls and stripping `async` from 8 functions, which is a wrong result shipped silently. The related risk-register scale rates a leaked secret or destroyed data as the highest impact, 5.

A fifth risk is a gap between what is installed and what the source says. ADR-0027 records a case where the installed plugin still allowed reads that the source now denies. The user accepts no such gap, because a fixed guard that is not live protects nothing in the session that fixed it.

A sixth group is agent conduct faults, which the plan treats as medical errors needing one general cure. Examples are citing files it never read (ADR-0028), deferring steps it could run itself or asking the user to do them (ADR-0042), holding finished work uncommitted and asking again (ADR-0030), and stopping to report when a correction named the fix (ADR-0044). The goal also bars a regex Stop check, so these must be cured without that tool.

A last group is cost and silent truncation. Mythos models were ruled out as too costly (ADR-0005), auto mode adds classifier cost (ADR-0002), and paid evals are capped and need approval (ADR-0019, superseded by ADR-0105). Skill descriptions over the listing cap are cut silently, which ADR-0023 handles by setting the cap to 200 and adding a linter.

END-OF-REPLY

Start by reading, in the order goal.md gives. Open `plans/rebuild/README.md` first, because it is the map: the layout, the eleven blocks, the routing rules, the item format and the attribution forms. Then read `prd/README.md` for scope and what is out, the `prd/<block>.md` file for the block you will work on, `arc42/02_architecture_constraints/` for fixed limits, `arc42/06_runtime_view/` for the algorithms, the relevant ADRs, and the matching `risk-register/<block>.md`. Read pointed-at files in slices for what the task needs, not in full (ADR-0029), and never claim a read you did not do.

Next, set up the working ground. Be on the branch `feat/claudetto-2.1.325-reinstantiation` and have a vanilla Claude Code 2.1.327 install to test against. Check the baseline at commit `088a227c`, since the building-block view describes what exists there, and look at the `plugins/` tree for the block you are picking up. If the install version or branch differs, resolve that before touching anything.

Then pick one block and work its checkboxes in order. For each `- [ ]` item, treat the requirement and its acceptance check as the contract. Before relying on any fact about Claude Code, verify it with a probe on `claude` 2.1.327 and record the probe name, version, date and command as the item's attribution. Every item needs a source in one of the README's forms, and you write no item without one. If the answer depends on something only the user knows, including what is worthwhile against vanilla 2.1.327, ask through `AskUserQuestion` instead of guessing.

Build the smallest thing that meets the acceptance check, keeping to the standing rules: files small and split by concern, no hyphenated file families, no benchmarks or planner or component swaps, no Fable or Opus as a subagent model, the advisor tool disabled, and no regex Stop check or constraint ledger. A component ships only if it beats vanilla Claude Code plus the model on a measured check (ADR-0177). Prefer the Mod route first, then a classic hook, skill or settings key (ADR-0009), and deny with the exact form instead of rewriting tool input (ADR-0025).

Tick an item only when its acceptance check passes, and name the command and its result in the commit. Commit your own work in separate Conventional Commits once the user has allowed it (ADR-0030). Do not merge, tag or release until the user says go (ADR-0032).

When you hit an agent fault, record it in `risk-register/<block>.md` as a medical error with one general cure across subsystems, not a one-off patch. Items that fall away go to `prd/README.md` scope Out with a reason.

Finally, dogfood. Install claudetto on the vanilla install, use it on itself, and fix what that shows, repeating until nothing is left to align. The work is done when every checkbox is ticked or moved to scope Out, `claude plugin test` passes, and a dogfood session shows no open risk at Likelihood 3 or higher.

END-OF-REPLY
